chapters.caption: The Ashmolean on Beaumont Street — Charles Cockerell's neoclassical building, opened in 1845
chapters.directions: Enter through the main entrance on Beaumont Street. Pick up a floor plan at the welcome desk — you'll want it — then head down to the Lower Ground Floor to start with the Ashmolean Story.
chapters.text: Welcome to the museum that invented museums. In 1683, the Ashmolean opened its doors to the public — and that word, public, was the revolution. Before this, collections of interesting objects lived in private houses, shown to friends and visiting scholars. Here, anyone who paid a small fee could walk in and look. It is often called the world's first public museum, and it's certainly Britain's. The collection began with John Tradescant and his son, royal gardeners and tireless travellers who assembled a famous 'cabinet of curiosities' in London — stuffed animals, exotic plants, weapons, coins, wonders. The antiquarian Elias Ashmole acquired it (in circumstances the Tradescant family disputed, loudly, but that's another story), gave it to Oxford University, and the museum took his name. The building you're standing in is the second home: Charles Cockerell's grand neoclassical pile from 1845, fronting Beaumont Street. Behind that classical façade, a major rebuild completed in 2009 doubled the gallery space with light-filled modern floors stacked behind and beneath the old building — so don't trust the modest street frontage; this place is a TARDIS holding half a million years of human history. General admission is free. Our route: start with the museum's own story downstairs, climb through the ancient world, cross Asia, finish with European art — and end, literally, on the roof.
chapters.title: Welcome — The World's First Public Museum

chapters.caption: Life after death in ancient Egypt — among the finest pre-Dynastic collections outside Cairo
chapters.directions: From the Ashmolean Story, head to the Ground Floor galleries for Ancient Egypt and Sudan (Galleries 22–27), then continue to the Greek and Roman rooms nearby.
chapters.text: Head into the Egypt galleries and slow down — this is one of the great Egyptian collections in Europe, and its particular glory is the stuff most museums don't have: pre-Dynastic Egypt, the thousands of years before the pharaohs. The Ashmolean holds the most significant collection of pre-Dynastic material outside Cairo, much of it from the pioneering excavations of Flinders Petrie and his teams, who more or less invented scientific archaeology in Egypt. Look for the delicately carved palettes, the beaded dresses, the pottery painted with boats and dancers from a world still inventing itself. Then the pharaonic material lands with full force: statues, coffins, jewellery, and mummies — including the mummified dead displayed with the grave goods they expected to use in the afterlife, which was less an ending than a change of address. Find the display on life after death and notice how practical the Egyptians were about eternity: food, furniture, servants in model form, even board games. The museum is candid, in its labels, about the colonial context of this collecting — excavated material was divided under British administration, which is how so much of Egypt ended up in Oxford. Reading those labels is part of the visit; the museum doesn't hide it, and neither should we. Give these rooms time — they reward it more than any quick march-past suggests.
chapters.title: Ancient Egypt — Before and Beyond the Pharaohs

chapters.caption: Greek and Roman sculpture — the Arundel Marbles and 2,500 years of Mediterranean art
chapters.directions: Continue on the Ground Floor to the Cast Gallery (Gallery 14), in one of the original 19th-century spaces off the main sculpture gallery.
chapters.text: From Egypt, walk into the Greek world — and notice the Ashmolean's trick: on this floor, civilisations are arranged to talk to each other across the Mediterranean, because that's how the ancient world actually worked. Start with the Aegean galleries: the museum's holdings from ancient Crete are among the most important outside Greece, much of it from Sir Arthur Evans, the archaeologist of Knossos — the man who uncovered the palace of the legendary King Minos and named the Minoans. Look for Cycladic figures, those eerily modern abstract marble forms from 2800 BC and earlier, which look like they were carved by a contemporary sculptor. Then the Greek and Roman sculpture gallery, home to the Arundel Marbles — classical sculptures collected in the 1600s by the Earl of Arundel, among the first great antiquities collections in England. Among them, keep an eye out for the portrait busts and the inscribed stones; the Ashmolean's collection of Greek inscriptions is a research treasure. The Rome gallery takes the story to an empire: portrait heads with every wrinkle of power preserved, coins, glass, and the material of daily Roman life. What's lovely here is the scale — these are intimate galleries, not warehouse halls, and you can stand nose-to-nose with a Roman emperor. He won't mind. He's had 2,000 years of it.
chapters.title: The Greek and Roman World — Marbles, Minoans, and Emperors

chapters.caption: Western Art galleries — Turner, the Pre-Raphaelites, and the Alfred Jewel nearby
chapters.directions: From the Cast Gallery, head up through the Asian Crossroads levels to the Western Art galleries on the upper floors (European Art, Level 3M).
chapters.text: Now climb to the Western Art galleries, where the Ashmolean quietly keeps one of the finest collections of drawings and paintings in Britain — many visitors, astonishingly, never make it up here. The painting highlights run from Italian Renaissance panels through to the moderns, but the collection has two particular claims on your attention. First, the drawings: the museum holds an extraordinary cabinet of works on paper, including drawings by Michelangelo and Raphael — fragile things, shown in rotation under low light, and if any are on display during your visit, stop everything and look. A Raphael drawing is as close as you can get to watching a Renaissance mind think. Second, the British art: the Ashmolean is a stronghold of the Pre-Raphaelites, the brotherhood of young Victorian painters — Rossetti, Millais, Holman Hunt — who rebelled against academic art from right here in Oxford's orbit. And look for Turner's watercolours and the famous view of Oxford's High Street. Also on these upper levels, don't miss two small objects with giant stories: the Alfred Jewel, a dazzling gold-and-enamel piece from the age of Alfred the Great, inscribed 'Alfred ordered me to be made'; and, nearby in the England galleries, Guy Fawkes's lantern — said to be the very lantern he was carrying when arrested under Parliament in 1605. From Raphael to the Gunpowder Plot in two rooms: that's the Ashmolean in a nutshell.
chapters.title: Western Art — Raphael Drawings, Pre-Raphaelites, and Turner

chapters.caption: Eastern Art — Chinese ceramics, Japanese prints, Islamic art and the samurai armour
chapters.directions: Continue through the Eastern Art galleries on Levels 1 and 2, then head down to the Lower Ground Floor for the Money Gallery (Gallery 7).
chapters.text: Cross now into the Eastern Art galleries, arranged — in the Ashmolean's post-2009 logic — as 'Asian Crossroads,' because Asia's cultures traded ideas along the Silk Roads just as the Mediterranean world did downstairs. The Chinese collection is a headline in itself: the museum's holdings of Chinese greenwares are described as the largest outside China, and its collection of modern Chinese painting is among Europe's finest. Look for the celadon ceramics — that sea-green glaze the Chinese perfected a thousand years ago — and the painted scrolls, where a whole landscape unrolls in a few brushstrokes. The Japanese galleries bring prints, lacquer, and one of the museum highlights everyone photographs: a full suit of samurai armour, all lacquered plates and silk cord, beautiful and faintly menacing. Then Islamic art: ceramics, metalwork and tiles from a civilisation that, when Europe was in its early medieval centuries, led the world in mathematics, medicine, and sheer gorgeousness of design. Notice the geometry — patterns that could extend to infinity, art as mathematics. The Indian galleries round it out with sculpture and textiles of astonishing richness. Take the long view for a second: you've now walked from Egypt to China in one building, arranged not as separate silos but as one connected human story. That was the 2009 rebuild's whole idea, and up here, it works.
chapters.title: Eastern Art — Silk Roads, Celadon, and Samurai

chapters.caption: The Cast Gallery — plaster casts of Greek and Roman masterpieces, some finer than the weathered originals
chapters.directions: From the Cast Gallery, head down to the Lower Ground Floor for the Money Gallery (Gallery 7).
chapters.text: Step into the Cast Gallery and enjoy the change of light and scale: row upon row of white plaster giants, gods and athletes and emperors, glowing in one of the original 19th-century rooms of Cockerell's building. These are plaster casts — exact copies — of famous Greek and Roman sculptures scattered across the museums of Europe, assembled from the 1700s onward so that Oxford students could study the classical world without leaving Beaumont Street. In the age before photography and cheap travel, cast collections like this were serious scholarly infrastructure; almost every great university had one, and almost all of them were later thrown out as unfashionable. The Ashmolean kept its — over 1,000 casts — and time has made them precious for an unexpected reason: many were moulded from originals that have since been damaged by acid rain and pollution, so in places the Oxford plaster preserves details the marble in Athens or Rome has lost. The cast is now, sometimes, the better document. Look for the Kritios Boy, the calm, revolutionary statue from about 480 BC that first showed a figure standing with his weight shifted — the moment Greek sculpture learned to relax. And just enjoy the room itself: it's the most atmospheric in the museum, a Victorian gallery that survived the rebuild untouched, and on a quiet morning it feels like a garden of sleeping gods.
chapters.title: The Cast Gallery — A Garden of Plaster Gods

chapters.caption: The Money Gallery — coins from the first Lydian issues to the modern world, in the Heberden Coin Room's home
chapters.directions: Head back up to the ground floor and out — or linger: the galleries are free, and re-visiting a favourite room is the Ashmolean way.
chapters.text: Down on the Lower Ground Floor, the Money Gallery takes something you handle every day and makes it strange and wonderful. The Ashmolean's coin collection — centred on the Heberden Coin Room — is one of the foremost in the world, and this gallery tells the whole biography of money: from the first coins struck in Lydia (in modern Turkey) in the 7th century BC, stamped lumps of electrum that changed commerce forever, through Greek city-state coins that doubled as tiny civic advertisements — Athens' owl, stamped on silver from the Laurion mines, was the dollar of its day. Roman coins were mass media: an emperor's face and message in every purse in the empire, propaganda you could spend. Look for the displays on money before and beyond coins — cowrie shells, metal bars, paper — and on the moments money breaks: debasement, forgery, inflation. If you're visiting on a Saturday, check for the hands-on coin-handling sessions, where volunteers let you hold real historic coins; there's something quietly thrilling about a 2,000-year-old coin sitting in your palm, still doing the job it was made for — being held, weighed, and wondered at. Money is trust made physical, and this gallery, better than any other I know, shows you the physical part.
chapters.title: The Money Gallery — The Biography of Coins

chapters.caption: The rooftop terrace — Oxford's spires from above the Ashmolean
chapters.directions: From the Money Gallery, ride the lift to Level 4 — the rooftop restaurant and terrace — for the final stop.
chapters.text: End your visit the way the building wants you to: on the roof. The Ashmolean's rooftop restaurant and terrace sit on Level 4, above Cockerell's classical façade, and the terrace looks out over Oxford's skyline — the dreaming spires doing their thing, with the Randolph Hotel across the street and the towers and domes of the colleges spread around you. It's a working restaurant (book ahead at busy times if you want lunch), but the terrace is also just a place to sit with a coffee and let the museum settle. And do let it settle, because the Ashmolean asks something of you that bigger museums don't: it asks you to connect. You've walked from pre-Dynastic Egypt to modern Chinese painting, from Roman emperors to Raphael's drawings to Guy Fawkes's lantern, in a building that invented the very idea of a public museum in 1683 — and that is still, today, a working university museum where researchers use these objects daily. If the weather turns or your feet give out, the café downstairs and the shop are both good. And remember the museum's greatest luxury: it's free, and it's all still here tomorrow. Oxford rewards a slow museum. You've done it properly.
chapters.title: The Rooftop Terrace — Coffee Above the Spires

chapters.caption: Half a million years in one building — the Ashmolean at dusk
chapters.directions: Exit onto Beaumont Street. The Bodleian, Radcliffe Square and Broad Street's museums are a few minutes' walk east.
chapters.text: A quick word before you step back out onto Beaumont Street, because the Ashmolean rewards a strategy: you cannot see half a million years in one visit, and you shouldn't try. What you've done today is the highlights spine — the museum's own story, Egypt and the classical world, the Cast Gallery, Asia, Western art, and money. If you have a second hour another day, the museum's own '10 highlights in an hour' trail (on the floor plan) and the special exhibitions on Level 3 are the natural sequel. And notice where you are: the Ashmolean sits in the heart of Oxford's museum quarter — the Bodleian and Radcliffe Square are a few minutes' walk east, the History of Science Museum (with Einstein's blackboard) is right across Broad Street, and the whole compact, golden city fans out from here. The Ashmolean was the first public museum in the world. Spending a morning inside the original — free, unhurried, surrounded by objects that stretch back before the pyramids — is one of the great quiet pleasures of England. Thanks for exploring it with me.
chapters.title: Wrap-Up — You Can't See It All (And That's Fine)

intro: The Ashmolean is the world's first public museum — opened in 1683, when the very idea that ordinary people could walk in and look at wonders was radical. Today it's Oxford University's museum of art and archaeology: half a million years of human creativity in one elegant building on Beaumont Street, and free. Our route climbs through time: the museum's own story, ancient Egypt and the classical world, the atmospheric Cast Gallery, Asia's Silk Road treasures, Western art from Raphael drawings to the Pre-Raphaelites, and the story of money itself — finishing on the rooftop terrace above Oxford's spires. Allow two hours, and don't try to see everything. Nobody can. That's the point.
mapNote: The Ashmolean stacks five levels behind its Beaumont Street façade. Lower Ground Floor: the Ashmolean Story, Money Gallery, Textiles, and Conservation. Ground Floor: the Ancient World — Egypt and Sudan, the Greek World, Rome, the Aegean, plus the Cast Gallery in the old building's east wing. Level 1: Asian Crossroads begins; Level 2: West Meets East (later Asian and Islamic art). Level 3: special exhibitions. Level 3M: European (Western) Art. Level 4: rooftop restaurant and terrace. Lifts and stairs sit in the modern central atrium — because the building weaves old and new wings, different parts of the same level aren't always connected, so use the atrium lifts to move between sections and check the floor plan.
practical: Admission to the permanent galleries is free; special exhibitions on Level 3 are ticketed. The museum is open daily, typically 10:00–17:00.
Pick up the free floor plan at the welcome desk — the building's mix of 1845 and 2009 wings is genuinely confusing without one, and it includes a '10 highlights in an hour' trail.
Don't try to see everything: half a million years of objects live here. Follow this guide's highlights route, then double back to whatever grabbed you.

The Cast Gallery and Western Art drawings are the connoisseur stops most visitors miss — if Raphael or Michelangelo drawings are on display, prioritise them; they're shown in rotation and not always out.
The rooftop restaurant is popular — book ahead for lunch, or just use the terrace for coffee and the view over Oxford.
Saturday coin-handling sessions in the Money Gallery let you hold real historic coins — free, drop-in, and great if you're visiting with kids.
Large bags may need to go in the lockers; travel light and keep your camera handy — photography (no flash) is allowed in most permanent galleries.
